Part A: Cleaning tweets¶

A1. Tweet features that break a standard tokenizer¶

Two problems are not about Twitter at all but about this file. First, the words "cancel" and "late" inside the tweet text were replaced by the label names "Cancelled Flight" and "Late Flight" somewhere before the data was published. Second, the rows labelled Delta are actually tweets sent to @JetBlue. Both are checked below.

# Fix both file problems before any analysis
df['airline'] = df['airline'].replace({'Delta': 'JetBlue'})

def repair_label_leak(text):
    text = re.sub(r'Cancelled Flight', 'cancel', text, flags=re.I)
    text = re.sub(r'Late Flight', 'late', text, flags=re.I)
    text = re.sub(r'Flight Booking Problems', 'book', text, flags=re.I)
    return text

print(repair_label_leak('Flight Cancelled Flightled and relate Flightd issues, reFlight Booking Problems Late Flightr today'))

Flight cancelled and related issues, rebook later today
In [6]:
# Cleaning, split into steps so the cost of each step can be measured in A4
def step1_normalise(text):
    text = html.unescape(text).replace('’', "'")
    text = repair_label_leak(text)
    return text.lower()

def step2_remove_links_handles(text):
    text = re.sub(r'http\S+', ' ', text)
    text = re.sub(r'@\w+', ' ', text)
    return text

def step3_letters_only(text):
    text = text.replace('#', ' ')                       # hashtag: keep the word
    text = re.sub(r"\bcan't\b", 'can not', text)
    text = re.sub(r"\bwon't\b", 'will not', text)
    text = re.sub(r"n't\b", ' not', text)               # didn't -> did not
    text = re.sub(r'([a-z])\1{2,}', r'\1\1', text)      # sooooo -> soo
    text = re.sub(r'[^a-z\s]', ' ', text)               # emoji, numbers, punctuation
    return text

def basic_tokens(text):
    return step3_letters_only(step2_remove_links_handles(step1_normalise(text))).split()

for name in ['Emoji', 'Stretched word (sooo)', "Contraction (didn't)"]:
    example = df.loc[df['text'].str.contains(features[name]), 'text'].iloc[0]
    print(name, '->', basic_tokens(example))

df['basic_tokens'] = df['text'].apply(basic_tokens)

A1 answer

The chart shows that every tweet starts with an @handle, and a smaller share contain hashtags, links, HTML entities like &, emojis, contractions and stretched words like "heyyyy". A naive tokenizer that lowercases and splits on spaces keeps all of these as they are. It produces tokens like "@virginamerica.", "hour.", "please?", "&", a full t.co link, and emojis glued together like "☺️👍". The same word ends up as many different tokens because punctuation sticks to it, so counts are split and the vocabulary is inflated with junk.

My treatment of each feature is as follows. Handles are removed, because the airline handle is in every tweet and tells us the target, not the opinion (the airline is already a column). Links are removed because t.co codes carry no meaning. For hashtags I keep the word and drop the # symbol, because tags like #fail or #nomorevirgin carry opinion. HTML entities are converted back to normal characters. Stretched words are shortened to two letters so "sooooo" and "soooo" become one token. Contractions are expanded so "didn't" becomes "did not" and the negation survives as its own word. Emojis are dropped from the word tokens, but VADER in Part C reads the original tweet, so the emoji signal is not lost where it matters.

Two problems come from the file, not from Twitter. The words "cancel", "late" and "book" inside tweets were replaced with the label names "Cancelled Flight", "Late Flight" and "Flight Booking Problems", which creates broken words like "Cancelled Flightled" (cancelled) and "relate Flightd" (related). If left alone, the label leaks into the text and every frequency chart is distorted. I reverse the replacement. Also, the rows labelled Delta are tweets addressed to @JetBlue (1,999 of 2,222 start with @JetBlue), so I rename that airline to JetBlue for the rest of the lab.

vader = SentimentIntensityAnalyzer()

def vader_label(text, analyser=vader):
    c = analyser.polarity_scores(text)['compound']
    if c >= 0.05:
        return 'positive'
    if c <= -0.05:
        return 'negative'
    return 'neutral'

versions = {
    'Cleaned, standard stop list': df['basic_tokens'].apply(lambda t: ' '.join(w for w in t if w not in STOP_STANDARD)),
    'Cleaned, negations kept': df['basic_tokens'].apply(lambda t: ' '.join(w for w in t if w not in STOP_FINAL)),
}

rows = []
for name, texts in versions.items():
    pred = texts.apply(vader_label)
    neg = df['airline_sentiment'] == 'negative'
    rows.append({'version': name,
                 'overall\nagreement %': accuracy_score(df['airline_sentiment'], pred) * 100,
                 'negative tweets\ncaught %': (pred[neg] == 'negative').mean() * 100,
                 'negative tweets\nscored positive %': (pred[neg] == 'positive').mean() * 100})
stop_effect = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('version').round(1)
print(stop_effect)

ax = stop_effect.T.plot.bar(figsize=(8, 4), color=['#a6acaf', '#2e86c1'], rot=0)
ax.set_ylabel('%')
ax.set_title('Removing "not", "no", "nor" changes what VADER sees')
ax.legend(title='')
for c in ax.containers:
    ax.bar_label(c, fmt='%.1f')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

A2 answer

The standard NLTK list contains 40 negation words, including not, no, nor and every n't form. Negations are much more common in negative tweets (42.8%) than in neutral (13.9%) or positive tweets (11.1%), so they are part of how people complain. The examples show the damage: "not happy" becomes "happy", "not good enough" becomes "good enough", and "not impressed" becomes "impressed". The cleaned tweet now says the opposite of the original.

The effect on sentiment is measurable. When VADER scores the cleaned text with the standard list, agreement with the human labels is 49.6% and it catches 41.8% of negative tweets. Keeping the negations raises this to 53.6% and 48.9%, and the share of negative tweets wrongly scored as positive drops from 34.6% to 30.6%. My final stop-word list is the NLTK list with all negation words taken out. Airline names and filler words are added later in Part B, only for the single-word charts.

A3. Stemming vs lemmatization¶

In [10]:
stemmer = PorterStemmer()
lemmatizer = WordNetLemmatizer()

def lemma(word):
    return lemmatizer.lemmatize(lemmatizer.lemmatize(word), 'v')   # noun form first, then verb form

no_stop_tokens = df['basic_tokens'].apply(lambda t: [w for w in t if w not in STOP_FINAL])
vocab = collections.Counter(w for t in no_stop_tokens for w in t)

compare = pd.DataFrame({'word': list(vocab.keys()), 'count': list(vocab.values())})
compare['stem'] = compare['word'].apply(stemmer.stem)
compare['lemma'] = compare['word'].apply(lemma)

sizes = pd.Series({'No reduction': compare['word'].nunique(),
                   'Lemmatization': compare['lemma'].nunique(),
                   'Porter stemming': compare['stem'].nunique()})
print(sizes)

disagree = compare[compare['stem'] != compare['lemma']].sort_values('count', ascending=False)
print()
print('Most frequent words where the two methods disagree:')
print(disagree.head(15).to_string(index=False))

A3 answer

After stop-word removal the vocabulary has 10,993 unique words. Lemmatization reduces it to about 8,860 and Porter stemming to about 8,330. Stemming shrinks the vocabulary more, but it does this by cutting word endings with rules, so many results are not real words: service becomes "servic", airline becomes "airlin", please becomes "pleas" and flying becomes "fli".

Some stems change the meaning, which is worse than looking odd. Customer becomes "custom", which is a different word, so "customer service" turns into "custom servic". United becomes "unit", which loses the airline name (lemmatization gives "unite", which is also wrong, but airline names are removed in Part B anyway). Lemmatization keeps customer, service and airline as they are, and still merges the forms that matter here: cancelled and delayed become cancel and delay, and flying becomes fly. It has one small fault (us becomes "u"), but "us" is a stop word and is removed anyway.

I chose lemmatization. The final audience is a non-technical Director, so the words on the charts must be readable, and the extra 530 words that stemming removes are not worth charts that say "servic" and "custom".

A4 answer

The vocabulary falls from 30,105 raw tokens to 8,838 at the end. The biggest drop is the letters-only step (24,668 to 11,122), and almost all of that is good: the same word with different punctuation attached, links, numbers and emojis were each counted as separate words. Lowercasing and dropping links and handles remove another 5,400 junk entries.

The length cost is concentrated in stop-word removal, which roughly halves the tweet from 16.3 to 8.9 words. That is expected, because tweets are full of words like "to", "the" and "my". It is the step where the meaning risk sits, which is why the negations were kept in A2.

Only 21 tweets become empty, all after stop-word removal. They are mostly neutral replies like "@united you too!" or "@united I have." whose meaning depended on an earlier tweet, so nothing analysable was lost. I do not think any step went too far for word counting. The step that would have gone too far is the standard stop list, because it reverses meaning in negated tweets. The other loss to note is emojis: they are dropped from the word tokens, which is fine for frequency charts but would be too much for sentiment, so VADER reads the original text.

Part B: Words and phrases¶

B1. Airline names and filler dominate the raw counts¶

In [14]:
FILLER = {'get', 'got', 'amp', 'im', 'would', 'one', 'go', 'also', 'flight', 'fly', 'still', 'could'}
DOMAIN_STOP = AIRLINE_NAMES | FILLER

def top_words(token_lists, n=15):
    return pd.Series(collections.Counter(w for t in token_lists for w in t)).nlargest(n)

raw_top = top_words(df['text'].str.lower().str.split())
clean_top = top_words(df['tokens'])
final_top = top_words(df['tokens'].apply(lambda t: [w for w in t if w not in DOMAIN_STOP]))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 5))
for ax, s, title, color in zip(axes, [raw_top, clean_top, final_top],
                               ['Raw text', 'After Part A cleaning', 'After removing airline names and filler'],
                               ['#a6acaf', '#5d6d7e', '#2e86c1']):
    ax.barh(s.index[::-1], s.values[::-1], color=color)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel('Count')
plt.tight_layout()

B1 answer

In the raw text the top words are "to", "the", "i", "a", "for" followed by "@united", "@usairways" and "@americanair". The chart tells us nothing about what customers say. After the Part A cleaning the filler is gone, but "flight", "get" and "fly" still sit at the top because almost every tweet about an airline mentions flying. After also removing airline names and a short list of filler words (get, got, amp, im, flight, fly, would and similar), the top words become real topics: not, thank, no, hour, delay, service, cancel, help, customer, call, bag, wait and hold.

Every single tweet contains an airline handle (100%). This tells us how the data was collected: someone searched Twitter for tweets that mention the six airline accounts, not a random sample of tweets about air travel. So the dataset only holds people who chose to tag the airline, usually to complain or ask for help. It also means the airline name is a collection label, not something the customer is saying, which is why it has to be removed before counting.

B2 answer

The butterfly chart compares the share of each group that uses the most common words. Words like flight, get, service, customer, help and time appear in both positive and negative tweets at similar rates, because both groups talk about flights and service. Raw frequency fails for two reasons. First, these shared topic words are the most common words overall, so they top both lists and hide the differences. Second, there are 9,178 negative tweets and only 2,363 positive ones, so raw counts make almost every word look "negative" simply because that group is four times larger.

TF-IDF fixes both problems. It lowers the weight of words that appear in many tweets of every kind, and taking the mean per tweet within each group removes the group-size effect. The words that truly separate the groups are thank, great, love, awesome, best, appreciate and amaze on the positive side, and not, hour, no, cancel, delay, hold, call, wait, bag and minute on the negative side. The negative words describe time lost and failed contact, while the positive words are almost all thanks and praise.

B3. Phrases in negative tweets¶

In [17]:
def top_ngrams(texts, n, k):
    cv = CountVectorizer(ngram_range=(n, n), token_pattern=r'\b\w+\b')
    counts = cv.fit_transform(texts).sum(axis=0).A1
    return pd.Series(counts, index=cv.get_feature_names_out()).nlargest(k)

bigrams = top_ngrams(neg['clean_nonames'], 2, 20)
trigrams = top_ngrams(neg['clean_nonames'], 3, 15)

axes[1].barh(trigrams.index[::-1], trigrams.values[::-1], color='#922b21')

def phrase_check(phrase):
    has = df['clean_nonames'].str.contains(r'\b' + phrase + r'\b')
    parts = {w: vader.polarity_scores(w)['compound'] for w in phrase.split()}
    return {'phrase': phrase, 'tweets': has.sum(),
            '% negative': (df.loc[has, 'airline_sentiment'] == 'negative').mean() * 100,
            'VADER score of each word': parts}

B3 answer

Two phrases point to a specific operational problem that a single word would hide. "Hold hour" (134 tweets, 99% negative) shows that people are stuck on the phone for hours. The single words "hold" and "hour" are both neutral to VADER, and "hour" alone could mean a delay. "Miss connection" (89 tweets, 94% negative) shows that delays are causing missed connecting flights, which is a scheduling and rebooking problem, not only a late departure. Other useful phrases are "call back", "no one answer" and "lose bag", and the trigrams "worst customer service" and "call customer service" show the service complaints are about reaching someone.

A phrase that flips the sentiment of its parts is "no help". VADER scores "help" as positive (+0.40), but the pair appears in 42 tweets and 98% of them are negative. "Not helpful" (24 tweets, 100% negative) and "thank nothing", from "thanks for nothing" (19 tweets, 100% negative), work the same way: the positive word becomes a complaint once you see its partner.

One noise phrase also appears, "rt fleet fleek", which is a JetBlue meme being retweeted. It shows why n-gram lists still need a human to read them.

B4 answer

I would show the Director the bar chart. The word cloud encodes frequency as font size, which readers judge badly, and long words like "customer" look more important than short words like "hour" even when they are less frequent. Position on the cloud means nothing, colour is decoration, and there is no scale, so the Director cannot tell whether "delay" is twice as common as "bag" or only a little more. The bar chart encodes the same counts as length from a common baseline, which is the most accurately read channel in Cleveland and McGill's ranking, it is sorted, and every bar has its count.

The word cloud is still useful as a first look or a cover image, because it gives an impression of the theme quickly. For a decision about where to spend money, the Director needs to compare sizes, and only the bar chart supports that.

Part C: Can a sentiment tool replace manual reading?¶

C1. VADER compared with the human labels¶

C1 answer

VADER agrees with the human label on only 48.3% of tweets. That is worse than a rule that labels every tweet negative, which would agree 62.7% of the time. The overall figure looks like "about half right", but the confusion matrix shows the errors are not spread evenly.

VADER finds 91% of positive tweets, but it does this by calling too many tweets positive: 41% of negative tweets and 57% of neutral tweets are also scored positive. It catches only 42.7% of negative tweets. Neutral is the hardest class by recall (32.4%), because VADER gives a score to almost any tweet that contains a polite or emotional word, and true neutral questions like "can you check my flight" often include "please" or "thanks".

What the overall figure hides is that the class that matters most to the business, negative, is the one the tool misses most. When VADER does say negative it is usually right (about 90% precision), but it misses more than half of the complaints, so an automated team would never see them.

vader_air.lexicon.update({
    'delay': -1.8, 'delayed': -1.8, 'delays': -1.8, 'cancel': -2.2, 'cancelled': -2.2, 'canceled': -2.2,
    'cancellation': -2.2, 'late': -1.5, 'stuck': -2.0, 'stranded': -2.5, 'hold': -1.0, 'missed': -1.5,
    'rebook': -1.0, 'rebooked': -1.0, 'waiting': -1.0, 'lost': -2.0, 'diverted': -1.5, 'overbooked': -2.0,
    'thanks': 0.4, 'thank': 0.4, 'please': 0.0,
})

                       (df.loc[df['airline_sentiment'] == 'negative', 'vader'] == 'negative').mean()],
    'VADER + airline lexicon': [accuracy_score(df['airline_sentiment'], df['vader_air']),

overall agreement                 48.3                     53.6

C2 answer

I took the 500 tweets where the VADER score is furthest from the human label. 495 of them are negative tweets that VADER scored as strongly positive, so the important failure is one-directional. Each tweet was tagged with the causes whose cue words it contains (a tweet can have more than one).

The largest cause is airline problem words (37%). Words like delayed, cancelled, hold, stuck, waiting and hours are strongly negative in an airline context, but a general lexicon gives them zero or a small score, while the same tweet often contains a polite word that VADER scores as positive. Negation is second (32%), then politeness such as thanks and please (26%) and mixed feelings with "but" (14%). Clear sarcasm phrases are only 3%, although many of the politeness cases are really sarcasm, for example "they wouldn't let me on. Real nice of you! Just love your awesome service".

The fix I propose is a domain lexicon. I added airline words to VADER with negative scores (delay, cancel, stuck, stranded, hold, missed, lost and similar) and lowered the weight of "thanks" and "please" so courtesy does not outweigh the complaint. This raises agreement from 48.3% to 53.6% and the share of negative tweets caught from 42.7% to 51.5%. It helps but does not solve sarcasm or negation, which need a model trained on airline tweets rather than a word list.

   words VADER knows: {}

C3 answer

Tweet 1 is sarcasm. VADER sees "great", "thanks" and "best" (and even "united", which it scores positive because it treats it as an ordinary word), and these outweigh "delay". It scores +0.93, positive, while any passenger would read it as an angry complaint.

Tweet 2 is a counterfactual. "I would have loved" describes what did not happen, so the tweet is a list of failures (no wifi, dirty seat, unfriendly crew). VADER only counts "loved", "clean" and "smiled" and scores it +0.88, positive.

Tweet 3 has no emotional words at all. "Sat on the tarmac 4 hours", "rebooked" and "sleeping at gate B12 tonight" describe a terrible night, but none of these words are in the lexicon, so VADER scores exactly 0 and calls it neutral. This is the airline-word problem from C2, and it is the most dangerous one because the passenger who needs help most can write in a calm, factual way.

C4 answer

The file has an airline_sentiment_confidence column, and 71.3% of tweets have full confidence (1.0). Keeping only those tweets raises VADER's agreement from 48.3% to 52.4%, and every class improves: negative from 42.7% to 47.0%, neutral from 32.4% to 37.2% and positive from 91.0% to 94.3%. The label mix also changes: neutral drops from 21.2% to 14.8% because neutral is the label the human annotators were least sure about (47% of neutral labels have confidence below 0.7, compared with 18% of negative labels).

This matters because part of what looked like tool error was really disagreement between people. If humans cannot agree whether a tweet is neutral or negative, a tool cannot be blamed for missing it, and the "ground truth" for those tweets is closer to a guess. The fair test of the tool is on the high-confidence tweets, and even there VADER is well below an acceptable level, so the conclusion from C1 still stands. The finding also tells us to treat the neutral class carefully in any later analysis.

D1 answer

The data partly supports the Director. American has the largest customer service share: 39% of its negative tweets are Customer Service Issue, and US Airways is close at 36%. JetBlue (labelled Delta in the file) is the opposite case: only 21% customer service, but the highest operations share, with 34% of its complaints about late or cancelled flights. So if "one airline has a service problem and another an operations problem" means American and JetBlue, the data agrees.

The picture is not that clean for everyone. US Airways is high on both axes, so it has a service problem and an operations problem at the same time. United has the most negative tweets of any airline but is close to average on both measures, with its complaints spread more evenly, including lost luggage (10%). Virgin America stands out for booking problems (16%), which suggests its website. The test also rests on human-coded reasons, and "Can't Tell" takes 10 to 20% of each airline's complaints, so the shares are approximate.

United has the most negative tweets (2,633), so by raw count it looks like the worst airline. But it also receives the most tweets overall (3,822), and its negative share is 68.9%. US Airways has fewer negative tweets (2,263) but a higher negative share, 77.7%, the worst in the data. American also has a higher share than United (71.0%). At the other end, Southwest and JetBlue have more than 900 negative tweets each, which looks large, but they are less than half of their tweets.

I would report the share, with the count next to it. The share answers "how unhappy are the customers who tweet about this airline", which is the fair comparison between airlines of different size. The count answers "how many tweets does the response team have to handle", which matters for staffing, not for judging the airline. Showing only counts would make United look worst simply because it is the biggest.

D3 answer

Tweet volume roughly doubles on 22 and 23 February, but most of the spike is a collection problem rather than a real event. American has 0 or 1 tweets on each day from 17 to 21 February and then nearly 1,000 a day, so its tweets were only collected from the 22nd. Any trend line for American, and any total that includes it, jumps for that reason alone. The last day, 24 February, is also partial.

Leaving American out, there is still a real change. On 22 and 23 February the negative share rose for US Airways (75.6% to 82.1%), United (66.7% to 73.0%), JetBlue (41.1% to 47.6%) and Virgin America, JetBlue negative tweets more than doubled on the 22nd and US Airways nearly doubled. The reason mix barely changed (Late Flight and Cancelled Flight stay around 20% and 9%), so the spike is more complaints of the same kinds rather than a new kind of problem. There is also a daily pattern: about 56 to 60% of tweets are negative in the late morning, rising to 72 to 74% between 10 pm and 1 am, when passengers are stuck after the last flights.

The data does not let us say why the spike happened. There is no weather, flight schedule or operations data in the file, and the collection window changes during the week. A winter storm or a system outage could explain it, but that would have to be checked against flight records, not inferred from tweets.

D4. Which negative tweets to answer first¶

In [34]:
DISRUPTION = {'Cancelled Flight', 'Late Flight', 'Lost Luggage', 'Flight Booking Problems'}
URGENT = r'\b(stuck|strand\w*|tonight|today|now|right now|asap|gate|connection|missed|miss|overnight|still waiting|hours?)\b'

def priority_points(r):
    pts = 0
    pts += 3 if r['negativereason'] in DISRUPTION else 0
    pts += 2 if re.search(URGENT, r['vader_text'], flags=re.I) else 0
    pts += 1 if r['retweet_count'] > 0 else 0
    pts += 1 if r['compound'] <= -0.5 else 0
    return pts

negdf = df[df['airline_sentiment'] == 'negative'].copy()
negdf['points'] = negdf.apply(priority_points, axis=1)
negdf['priority'] = pd.cut(negdf['points'], bins=[-1, 2, 4, 7], labels=['P3 normal', 'P2 soon', 'P1 answer first'])

D4 answer

My rule gives each negative tweet points. It gets 3 points if the complaint is a live travel disruption (Cancelled Flight, Late Flight, Lost Luggage or Flight Booking Problems), because the airline can still fix these while the passenger is travelling. It gets 2 points if the text shows the passenger is stuck right now (words like stuck, stranded, tonight, gate, connection, missed, hours, now). It gets 1 point if the tweet was retweeted, because others are seeing it, and 1 point if VADER finds strong negative language. A tweet with 5 or more points is P1 (answer first), 3 to 4 is P2 (answer soon) and the rest is P3.

This gives 1,483 P1 tweets (16% of negative tweets), 2,578 P2 and 5,117 P3. The P1 examples are the right kind of tweet, for example a passenger on hold for 40 to 50 minutes asking for an earlier flight tonight. I defend the rule because it puts problems that can still be solved ahead of general venting, and a reply to a stranded passenger can save a connection or a hotel night, while a reply to "worst airline ever" changes little. The points are simple enough for the team to understand and adjust.

The limit is that the reason column was filled by humans after the fact. In live use the reason would have to come from a keyword or model classifier, which would make mistakes like the ones in Part C, so the rule should be tested on new tweets before relying on it.

E1. How this dataset could mislead the airline¶

First, Twitter users are not passengers in general. They are younger and more online, and the people in this file chose to tag the airline, which people mostly do when something has gone wrong. The 62.7% negative share describes people who tweet at airlines, not how passengers feel.

Second, a small group of loud users carries a lot of weight. 24.2% of all tweets come from users who tweeted five or more times, and the most active account is JetBlueNews, a news bot, not a customer. One angry passenger with ten tweets counts ten times.

Third, the collection is uneven. American was only collected from 22 February, the Delta rows are JetBlue, and label words were pasted into the tweet text. Comparisons over time or between airlines inherit these errors. In addition, 93% of tweets have no coordinates, so nothing can be said about which airports or routes are affected.

The finding I trust least is the time trend in D3, because the collection window itself changes during the week. I also trust the airline-by-reason shares in D1 less than the overall picture, because they depend on human reason labels where "Can't Tell" is 10 to 20% and some reasons have only a few dozen tweets per airline.

E2. What would change with data from today¶

The airline ranking would likely change most. US Airways no longer exists (it merged into American in 2015) and Virgin America was absorbed by Alaska Airlines in 2018, so two of the six airlines are gone, and the others have changed their service since then.

The channel has changed too. Twitter is now X, many customers complain through airline apps, chat and other platforms, and airlines answer through direct messages, so public tweets are a smaller and different slice of customers. The phone hold complaints ("hold hour", "call back") may be lower where chat and app rebooking now exist.

The language would also change. Today's tweets would mention apps, Wi-Fi, bag fees and refunds more, use more emojis and new slang, and include more sarcasm, which makes the lexicon problems in Part C worse. What I expect to stay the same is the basic shape: complaints are mostly about delays, cancellations, lost bags and reaching customer service, and negative tweets far outnumber positive ones, because that is how people use a public complaint channel.

E3. Should the manual team be replaced by the tool?¶

I argue against replacing the team, and for using the tool to support it. The tool's failures are in exactly the place that matters. VADER agreed with the human labels on only 48% of tweets, worse than guessing "negative" every time, and it missed 57% of negative tweets. It is fooled by airline words it does not know, by negation, by politeness and by sarcasm, and the most urgent tweets, from stranded passengers writing calmly, often get a neutral score. Even with my airline lexicon it only catches about half of the complaints.

The tool does have strengths. It is instant, it reads every tweet, and when it says a tweet is negative it is right about 90% of the time. Combined with the priority rule from D4 and keyword alerts for words like cancel, stranded and missed connection, it can sort the queue so the team reads the most urgent tweets first instead of reading in order. That solves the Director's real problem, reacting days late, without trusting the tool with decisions it cannot make. The team can then become smaller over time, as a model trained on the airline's own labelled tweets is tested and shown to do better.

neg_users = df[df['airline_sentiment'] == 'negative']['name'].value_counts()
repeat = neg_users[neg_users >= 3]
print(f'Users with 3+ negative tweets: {len(repeat):,} ({len(repeat) / neg_users.size:.1%} of complaining users)')
print(f'Their share of all negative tweets: {repeat.sum() / neg_users.sum():.1%}')

bins = pd.cut(neg_users, bins=[0, 1, 2, 4, 100], labels=['1', '2', '3-4', '5+'])
tweets_by_bin = neg_users.groupby(bins).sum()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
ax.bar(tweets_by_bin.index.astype(str), tweets_by_bin.values, color='#7d3c98')
for i, v in enumerate(tweets_by_bin.values):
    ax.text(i, v + 50, f'{v:,}', ha='center')
ax.set_xlabel('Negative tweets sent by the same user')
ax.set_ylabel('Negative tweets')
ax.set_title('Insight 3: a group of unresolved customers keeps tweeting')
ax.set_ylim(0, tweets_by_bin.max() * 1.15)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Users with 3+ negative tweets: 907 (18.2% of complaining users)
Their share of all negative tweets: 45.2%

Part F insights¶

Insight 1. The customer service problem is largely a phone line problem.

Observation: 36.5% of all Customer Service complaints mention being on hold, calling or the phone, rising to 48% at US Airways and Southwest and 40% at American.

Evidence: the Insight 1 chart, and the phrases "hold hour" (134 tweets), "call back" and "no one answer" in B3.

Why it matters: these passengers already tried the official channel and gave up. They usually have a live problem, such as a cancelled flight, and long hold times turn one failure into two.

Recommended action: add a callback option and online or chat rebooking at US Airways, Southwest and American first, and post expected hold times on Twitter during disruptions.

Confidence and limits: fairly confident in the direction, because the pattern is large and consistent. The keyword match will miss some phone complaints and catch a few unrelated uses of "call", and the reason label is human-coded.

Insight 2. The data file has errors that an automated tool would quietly absorb.

Observation: 1,999 of the 2,222 tweets labelled Delta are addressed to @JetBlue, 1,552 tweets have label names pasted into their words, and American has only 4 tweets before 22 February.

Evidence: the Insight 2 chart and the checks in A1 and D3.

Why it matters: any vendor tool or dashboard built on this file would report the wrong airline, learn the labels from the text, and show a false spike for American. Decisions about which airline or which week is worst would be wrong.

Recommended action: before buying any sentiment tool, require a data audit step (airline check from the handle, scan for label text in the tweet, and a check that every airline covers the same dates), and repeat it for each new data pull.

Confidence and limits: very confident that the errors exist, because they can be seen directly in the text. I cannot tell where in the pipeline they were introduced.

Insight 3. A group of repeat complainers produces almost half of the negative tweets.

Observation: 907 users (18% of complaining users) sent three or more negative tweets, and together they wrote 45% of all negative tweets.

Evidence: the Insight 3 chart, which shows how many negative tweets come from users who tweeted once, twice, three to four times and five or more times.

Why it matters: a customer who tweets again and again is usually a case that was not solved after the first contact. These customers inflate the negative totals and are the ones most likely to go public elsewhere or switch airlines.

Recommended action: track each complaining user as a case. When the same person tweets a second time, move the case to a senior agent with authority to rebook or compensate, and measure the share of complaints solved on first reply.

Confidence and limits: confident in the numbers. Some repeat tweets are a long story split over several tweets rather than unresolved cases, and the data has no reply information, so I cannot prove the airline failed to respond.

One-page brief for the Director of Customer Experience¶

To: Director of Customer Experience Subject: What 14,640 airline tweets from February 2015 tell us

What customers complain about. The most common complaints are delays, cancellations, lost bags and, above all, not being able to reach anyone. "Customer service" is the most frequent phrase in negative tweets, and over a third of service complaints are about phone hold times, with phrases like "hold hour", "call back" and "no one answer". Praise is almost always short thanks for a specific good moment.

Can software replace the reading team? Not yet. The standard sentiment tool agreed with human readers on only 48% of tweets and missed more than half of the complaints. It is fooled by sarcasm, by "not", by polite words and by airline words like delayed and cancelled. Adding airline vocabulary helps, raising the share of complaints caught from 43% to 52%, but that is still too low to run unsupervised.

How the airlines compare. US Airways has the highest share of negative tweets (78%), ahead of American (71%) and United (69%). United has the most complaints in total only because it gets the most tweets. American's complaints lean toward customer service, JetBlue's toward delays and cancellations, and US Airways is high on both.

Where to act first. Fix the phone channel with callbacks and online rebooking, starting at US Airways, Southwest and American. Use the tool to sort the queue, not to replace people: answer first the tweets about live disruptions from passengers who say they are stuck now, which is about 1 in 6 complaints. Treat a customer's second complaint as an escalation, because 18% of complaining users wrote 45% of the negative tweets.

Cautions. Twitter users are not all passengers, the data covers only one week in 2015, and the file has errors (the Delta tweets are JetBlue, and American was only collected from 22 February). The direction of these findings is reliable; the exact percentages are not.
